title: Advanced Prompting Patterns for Code
description: Master chain-of-thought, few-shot, and role-based prompting techniques to get consistently better code from AI models.

data.text: Basic prompting gets you basic results. Advanced prompting patterns — chain-of-thought, few-shot examples, and role-based prompting — dramatically improve the quality, consistency, and reliability of AI-generated code. These techniques are borrowed from research on large language models but are directly applicable to coding tasks.

Chain-of-thought prompting asks the AI to reason through a problem step by step before giving the final answer. For code tasks, this means asking the AI to explain its reasoning about a bug or architecture decision before suggesting a fix. This produces higher-quality code because the AI has thought through the problem more carefully.

data.title: Chain-of-thought prompt for debugging
data.content:
Instead of: "Fix this bug"

Try: "I have a bug in this function. Before proposing a fix, please walk through the code step by step and explain what each part does. Then identify where the logic diverges from the intended behavior. Finally, propose a minimal fix with explanation."
data.code:
Chain-of-thought prompt:

"I have a bug in this function. Before proposing a fix, please walk through the code step by step and explain what each part does. Then identify where the logic diverges from the intended behavior. Finally, propose a minimal fix with explanation."

data.title: Use 'Let's think step by step'
data.text: The phrase 'Let's think step by step' is one of the most well-known chain-of-thought triggers. For code tasks, adapt it: 'Before writing the solution, explain your approach step by step.' This gives you a chance to correct the AI's reasoning before it writes code.

Few-shot prompting means giving the AI a few examples of the input-output pattern you want, then asking it to continue the pattern. For code generation, this is one of the most powerful techniques. If you want the AI to write functions in your project's style, show it one or two examples of existing functions as the pattern.

data.title: Few-shot prompt for consistent function style
data.content:
"Here are two examples of how we write API handler functions in this project:

Example 1:
[paste an existing handler]

Example 2:
[paste another existing handler]

Now write a new handler for DELETE /api/users/:id that follows the exact same patterns. Use our existing error handling and response formatting."
data.code:
Few-shot prompt:

"Here are two examples of how we write API handler functions in this project:

Example 1:
[paste an existing handler]

Example 2:
[paste another existing handler]

Now write a new handler for `DELETE /api/users/:id` that follows the exact same patterns. Use our existing error handling and response formatting."

data.text: Assigning a specific role to the AI at the start of a prompt changes how it responds. 'You are a senior TypeScript developer who prioritizes type safety' produces very different output than 'You are a quick-and-dirty scripting expert.' For production code, always assign a role that matches the quality bar you expect.

data.title: Effective roles for coding tasks:
items: "You are a senior TypeScript developer who values type safety and explicit error handling"
"You are a security-conscious backend engineer who reviews every line for vulnerabilities"
"You are a performance optimization expert who profiles before refactoring"
"You are a frontend accessibility specialist who ensures every component is screen-reader friendly"

data.text: Giving explicit constraints in your prompt produces more reliable results. Instead of asking for 'a good function,' ask for 'a function under 20 lines that handles null inputs gracefully and uses our existing error types.' Constraints narrow the solution space and reduce the chance of the AI generating something that does not fit your requirements.

For high-stakes code, ask the AI to verify its own output. 'Write a function that validates email addresses. After writing it, list any edge cases it does not handle and propose fixes.' This self-verification pattern catches many common bugs before you even run the code.

The most effective prompts combine multiple patterns. A strong prompt might start with a role, include a few-shot example, ask for chain-of-thought reasoning, specify constraints, and request self-verification. The exact combination depends on the task complexity — do not over-prompt simple tasks, but use multiple patterns for complex architectural work.

data.title: Combined pattern prompt
data.content:
"You are a senior backend engineer who writes clean, testable Node.js code.

Here is how we structure our service files:
[paste an example service file]

Task: Write a new UserService with methods: create, findById, update, delete. Follow the same patterns as the example. Before writing the code, outline your approach step by step. After writing, list any edge cases and how you handle them. Keep each method under 15 lines. Use our existing DatabaseError class for errors."
data.code:
Combined pattern prompt:

"You are a senior backend engineer who writes clean, testable Node.js code.

Here is how we structure our service files:
[paste an example service file]

Task: Write a new `UserService` with methods: `create`, `findById`, `update`, `delete`. Follow the same patterns as the example. Before writing the code, outline your approach step by step. After writing, list any edge cases and how you handle them. Keep each method under 15 lines. Use our existing `DatabaseError` class for errors."

data.title: Practice makes permanent
data.text: Advanced prompting patterns feel unnatural at first. Practice with low-stakes tasks — generate a utility function, not a critical payment system. As the patterns become second nature, apply them to higher-stakes work.

data.title: Advanced prompting patterns
points: Chain-of-thought: ask the AI to reason before answering
Few-shot: provide examples of the pattern you want
Role-based: assign a role that matches your quality bar
Constrained: specify limits and requirements explicitly
Self-verification: ask the AI to check its own work
